answer:
Dear SaaStr:  How does one sell software to a CIO?
It’s tough, but it can be done.
You need at least these things:
A very strong brand
An existing relationship with a customer or two that is happy and has gone deep
At least some sort of proof points / case studies
A true champion on their team
A long sales cycle (12+ months) to let you get there
If you don’t have any of this … then you’ll never make it into IT … unless your product solves a truly unique problem no other vendor does. Even then, it will take time.
Now if you do have something like this …
Then here are my learnings from having been acquired by Cisco Systems for $230m+ :
First, know when you’re getting close to making them money back. That may sound obvious, but it really isn’t all that often. Most startups selling to larger enterprises never even break out of “pilot mode” so they rarely ever see a real ROI. But what I learned was once we got to say $200k-$300k ARR per pilot, we could show we were saving more than it cost us. So that made it easy to scale up those pilots.
Second, find someone willing to bet his career on you. This always works, especially in tech. Find someone who believes enough in your startup to put her/his career on the line. And go help her/him win. They might not care as much about the financials, which means they won’t sweat every nickel-and-dime expense. And they’ll want to build a big business around you, too.
Third, understand the social contract. The enterprise buyer has invested heavily in a platform, workflow, process, etc. Once they’ve gone down a path, they tend to stay committed to it. So you have to earn the right to come in, displace part of the stack, and change processes. That takes time.

answer:
So one thing I've learned is that it's easy for folks, especially salespeople and others who have worked at bigger companies, they think they know how enterprise software works.
They think they understand all this. But they don't really get it until you work with real enterprises, or sell into them, as a founder yourself.
And one thing that many founders miss when they start out selling into the enterprise, which we'll come back to later, but just one little piece of advice here is they underestimate the power of the social contract within larger organizations.
What do I mean by the social contract? So most medium sized and large organizations are structured around these different departments. And each department has their own budget and priorities.
But more importantly, each department often reports up through the organization chart to one boss. Usually two bosses.
The functional leader, who cares deeply about what this team does, and then there's always a VP level manager above him that also owns those dollars.
Now imagine if your product was Salesforce.com. It would be owned primarily by the Chief Information Officer. That person might oversee $300 million worth of IT budgets across the company. A huge amount of money. A lot of priorities. But ultimately, that officer reports to the CEO.
That means he's got some flexibility to make discretionary purchases. There may be one or two areas where he can go off on his own and buy something without having to run it by everyone else. Maybe marketing has some extra budget. Or maybe it's part of a business unit, not necessarily under his control, but he knows he needs to invest there.
He wants to keep up with the competition. He doesn't want to look behind in the marketplace. He wants to stay ahead. So these officers and VPs have flexibility in their budgets.
But here's the catch -- they're constrained by the social contract with other people in the organization.

5.  Top quartile deal sizes grow faster than rest.
In other words, they’re driving towards enterprise customers, while still serving their core SMB base.

So there are two SaaS leaders we’ve covered that have been on fire during Covid.  One is Zoominfo,
which we’ve written quite a bit about.
The other is Monday.com, which I want to focus on today because it’s just one of those quiet SaaS winners.  It started off as an open source project called “dapulse” way back in 2012.  And then went Freemium and eventually paid like most apps do.
It took them 7 years to get their first million in revenue.  But once they got there — man they exploded:
$1m ARR in Year 8 (just before IPO)
$100m ARR in Year 12
$200m ARR in Year 13 (!)
$300m ARR in Year 14
$400m ARR in Year 15
$500m ARR in Year 16
And now approaching $600m in ARR by year-end!

#1.  90% GRR and 110% NDR Fuel The Engine At Scale.  A reminder to go long and invest in retention
.  With 120%+ NDR, any churn really hurts.  So let’s invest even more here.  Even if it seems hard, it can pay big dividends.  Not only does it fuel your growth engine, but it also fuels the magic of net negative churn.

#2.  70% Self-Serve Revenue Fuels The Growth Machine
.  While enterprise sales have grown faster since IPO, Monday still relies heavily on self-serve and smaller customers to grow.  We see many of us doing this these days, especially where possible.  HubSpot, Zendesk, Monday, and more rely on both segments.

answer:
Dear SaaStr:  How Can I Really Stand Out During an Interview?
Here’s how you can stand out in interviews:
Research and prepare for each interview as if it were your first. It is probably not.
Show up early and make sure everyone knows who you are before they start talking to anyone else. Dress well and be confident without being arrogant. A great way to do this — send them a note ahead of time telling them exactly what questions you’ll answer with specific examples.
Be honest but highlight achievements instead of shortcomings. Use metrics and data points when possible to support your claims. Share stories that show growth potential or ability to take on new challenges. Don’t just talk about past experiences—show how those skills could help the company move forward.
The best candidates find ways to connect their background directly to the role and company. If you’ve worked at companies similar to theirs, point out why you’re uniquely qualified based on shared values or approaches. Show that you understand where they’re coming from and what might work given their context. For example, “I noticed your focus on customer success—that aligns perfectly with my experience driving NRR improvements through proactive outreach.”
Highlight any unique value proposition (UVP) you bring beyond typical qualifications. This isn’t about bragging; it’s about showing how you solve problems differently than others would. In sales roles especially, emphasize any creative strategies you’d use to close deals faster or more efficiently. For instance, you could mention building strong relationships early on by offering valuable insights during demos rather than just pushing product features.

answer: So one thing that I've learned over many years as an investor and CEO is what makes for truly great candidates. And you might think it's all about domain expertise, but no, it's not that simple. It really isn't. But what are the things that make folks stand out? Because when we interview at scale, there are just so many people coming through the door. You want someone who stands out, especially on your management team. So let me share my learnings with you today. Number one, be curious. Be genuinely interested in why they're leaving their last role. Not "Oh, I love this company" or "I'm looking for something new." No, be specific. What was the experience like? Why did you leave? That shows curiosity. Don't be afraid to ask questions. This always surprises me because almost every time I see a candidate ask good questions during an interview process, I know I got a very strong candidate. Even if they don't have perfect answers to everything. Second, bring your own data. Bring metrics. Show me how you impacted revenue at your previous company. If you were an individual contributor, show me how much more quota you hit than anyone else. Tell me about the deals you closed personally. Bring proof points. Third, say exactly what job you're looking for. Don't tell me you'll take any sales role. Say you're looking to lead a team of five, that you want to manage two ICs under you, and you're excited to work with the VP of Sales directly. Being clear on what you're looking for is actually a strength, not weakness. Fourth, back up your claims with stories. When they say they built a sales process, ask them to walk you through three specific examples.

So we’ve all heard of Salesforce and have probably used its products.  And Informatica is one of their top partners.
And now it’s been acquired for an astonishing $8B — after going public twice!
Let that sink in.
What did they do?  They started back in 1989 (!) as “Informix Software” doing database software.  Yes, you read that right.  It was founded way back then.
Fast forward to today, they are still focused on data management and analytics, but this time more around enterprise data management.  More on what that means here:
How Informatica Went From $1m ARR To A $7B+ Acquisition | SaaStr
But really, from almost any angle, Informatica looks like … just plain crazy.  Crazy growth at first (yes, in B2D), crazy downgrades, crazy bankruptcies, crazy ups-and-downs.  You could write a book on them alone.
But let me tell you two things about Informatica:
First,
it had zero MRR when I invested in 2005 or so
.  Zero!  Just as I closed my seed fund, I met with Informatica CEO Gaurav Vaidya who had bought the company out of bankruptcy.  He said he’d never raised VC before.  I told him to raise some money if he needed it, because I knew how hard it was to start over.
Second,
I tried to buy Informatica myself years later
.  In fact, my very last acquisition offer ever. 🙂   The price ended up being too high though.  But boy would that have been cool.
Wow, there’s your crazy story of Informatica.  Started in 1989.  Had no revenue until 1996.  Then hit $100m in revenue fast, but then crashed.  Declared bankruptcy.  Bought itself back and went public again.  Got taken private again.  And finally, 32 years later, got acquired for $8 billion.  Wow.
A crazy ride indeed!!

So we’ve talked a lot on SaaStr over the years, and I thought we’d summarized all the key trends.  But then … Covid hit.
And with it, an explosion of new sales reps into Zoom calls that they never had before.   This is changing SaaS forever.  And not just for this year — but for how we sell software going forward.
Because most buyers don’t want to go back to their old ways once they see the power of selling remotely:
The number one change?  Buyers love remote demos and discovery sessions.  They can do them at home, or in any case, without having to get dressed up and leave their office.

But the best part is, because folks aren’t as tired from traveling anymore (not all the way), and they often have more bandwidth than ever since they’re working from home …
You can do so much more.  So many more deals close faster.  So many more questions answered by video during the buying process.
It’s great.  It’s like magic.

So with public multiples at record lows for all but a handful of Cloud leaders like Snowflake and MongoDB (and even they are under pressure), this is top-of-mind for many SaaS founders today.
Should you worry if your investors do?
I think so — to some extent.
Why would I say that?  Well:
First, it’s tough when folks aren’t seeing their investments going up in value
. That can lead to less support on your cap table.
Second,
many VC funds have 10%-20% of their capital committed to later-stage rounds
. If those rounds don’t happen … well …
Third,
your board meetings may get tougher now
. If things aren’t growing as fast as before, or at least not quite as much as before, there will be more tension around whether you raise enough cash each year. And if multiples stay low, more questions around how long your runway truly is.
But here’s my take:
You shouldn’t obsess too much over what VCs are saying publicly on social media etc.
Mostly, we’re worried because we’re paid based on relative performance vs other venture firms
. We’ve also invested a lot in our own brand over time.
A few thoughts on where we stand from me personally below:

May 12, 2022

If you haven’t raised any new money since Q1’21, you probably need to
. It doesn’t matter if you were “cash-flow positive”. Yes, you may have been able to pay salaries out of cash, and hire a bunch of engineers. But the burn rate isn’t really decreasing anymore, especially once you start hiring again.

But they are still zombies.  Zombies for growth.
Because if your net revenue retention is below 100% — you can grow, even if slowly.  But it won’t be enough.
The problem here is two-fold:
First, you’ll never build a unicorn unless you start recruiting better talent
.  Folks want to join winners and doers.  Not zombie SaaS startups that aren’t going anywhere fast.
Second, you’ll run out of runway.   This might take years (or even decades), but eventually, you will run out of cash building software nobody wants more of.  Even if your NRR isn’t terrible, if customers just don’t want to buy more seats, it may only really fuel growth for so long.

Don’t give up.  There are many examples where folks turned around a low-growth NRR engine into something great again.
But first, make sure everyone knows what happened
.  This can help rebuild confidence in a team when times seem tough.  Everyone knows how bad things are today, but no one always understands why.  Maybe now is the time to finally share some real data on where we’ve fallen behind.  And then show a way forward.
Hire someone who has done it before
.  Someone whose job was to drive upsells from $0.01m ARR to $1.00m+ ARR.  That’s a skill set.  Hire them.
Double-down on customer success
.  It’s easy to cut CS budgets when growth slows down.  Don’t do this.  Instead, double-down on CS.  The best CSMs know how to sell too.  At least a bit.  Make sure every single top account has a truly excellent CSM.
Be honest with yourself and your investors
.

Even if everything else is great, your NRR falls 1 or 2 points every quarter after Year One unless you take action. And so before long, you'll find yourself in a world where you need twice as many leads to get half as much revenue per lead than last year. That creates massive stress in the team, especially in the sales team. Because now you're under pressure to hit quota and it feels impossible.

Dear SaaStr: How do you handle it when your finance team doesn’t meet deadlines?
I’m not sure this is quite what’s happening here, but … 😉  Let me share my learnings.
First, let me tell you — we all make mistakes in our careers and roles that lead to missing important dates. Even as CEO of a $100m+ ARR company today, if there was one thing I’d say I still struggle with, it’s getting things out on time.
The good news for founders is most VCs don’t expect perfect financial plans and models. But they often want them monthly or even weekly in some cases (e.g., at Rocketship). And every VC wants them done by the start of each month.

. This is super common after IPOs, M&A, etc. But during normal times? It shouldn’t happen more than once. You have to help her get up to speed ASAP.

What Is the Cowan Paradox? Named after economist Roy Cowan (who first identified it in his 1976 paper “Effects of Technological Change on Productivity Growth”), this paradox describes what happens when technology increases productivity but doesn’t reduce workload. In fact, it often leads to an increase in output per worker.
This sounds counterintuitive at first. If a factory robot can produce five times as much as human workers, shouldn’t we expect fewer employees needed overall?
Nope.
Here’s what actually happens:
Management figures out ways to add new products, lines, shifts, quality improvements, or other outputs from those same robots. Or even better … management finds a way to grow the pie so there is room for everyone to get more output from the same number of resources. Often by growing headcount right back up again!
So instead of cutting jobs, companies hire more people to take advantage of the increased efficiency. It’s a vicious cycle where every technological improvement creates pressure to expand production further, which then requires more labor to maintain the growth trajectory.
The result:
Productivity goes through the roof while employment stays flat.

So we’ve been talking for years now on SaaStr, and I know this will sound a little weird coming from me because you’ll hear me say all the time that go buy something off the shelf if it’s available.
But there are more and more products where building your own solution yourself is better than buying one off the shelf.
There are two categories really of solutions today. And they’re kind of opposite of each other.
The first is an N=2 product. That means you need at least two people to use it and understand how to use it.
And the second is an N=1000 or more product. So here’s my point. For most of us, those N=2 apps don’t exist anymore. They haven’t existed for a long time.
Because almost any app these days has to be so sophisticated, so complex, with so many features built into them that no human being could possibly learn how to use it without having worked at the company that created it before.
It just can’t happen anymore.
Now, I’m not saying every single person who uses an app needs to work at the company that made it. But there are certain types of functionality and types of software out there — I think increasingly — especially in B2B, but certainly in vertical markets like healthcare and finance and manufacturing, whatever it may be — where you have to roll up your sleeves and build some version of it yourself.
Not always code-it-from-scratch yourself, but maybe buy an agentic solution that does what you want it to do.
Maybe use a tool like Replit or Lovable or something else that allows you to create a custom application for free.
Or maybe hire a developer that doesn’t cost $200 an hour. Maybe find someone very good that costs $50 an hour.
You might get the thing done for less money than you spend getting an enterprise deal going on Salesforce or HubSpot or whoever.
That’s actually happening more often nowadays.
